text:
Droit de la famille — 192549

2019 QCCS 5328

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTRÉAL

No:

500-04-073317-183

DATE:

December 10, 2019

_____________________________________________________________________

BY

THE HONOURABLE

CHRISTIAN
IMMER, J.S.C.

_____________________________________________________________________

M. G.

Plaintiff

v.

A. B.

Defendant

_____________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

_____________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

The father seeks shared custody of his four year
son and that the alimony which he pays to the mother, the defendant, on his
son’s behalf, be revised accordingly. He also requests that his son be
registered in the denominational A School in the fall of 2020.

[
2
]

The mother contests these requests. She insists
on maintaining the accesses as they are. She further wants her son to be
inscribed in B elementary school, which is part of the A School Board.

1.

COntext

[
3
]

The parties are wed on March 29, 2015. The mother
gives birth to the couple’s only son, X, […] later.

[
4
]

The couple ceases to live together on August 3,
2018, when the mother definitely moves out of the family’s home with her son.

[
5
]

The father consistently asks from then on for shared
custody of the child. No agreement is found on such shared custody in August
2018, but the parties agree on the modalities of a two month transition period.
[1]
The father will pick up the
child from day care when the maternal grandparents do not do so. The child will
also spend Shabbat with him and his family on Friday evenings before bringing
him home to this mother at noon on Saturday.

[
6
]

In conformity with this agreement, he picks his
son up from daycare in August 2018 at a rate of two to five times a week and his
son stays at his house every Friday afternoon to Saturday at noon. In
September, the pick-ups at the day care stabilize to twice a week and the child
continues to sleep over on Friday nights.
[2]

[
7
]

In late September 2018, wanting to increase time
with his son, he asks that they transition to shared custody as he feels is the
agreement and requests that a transition occur over a “number of months they
can agree on”.
[3]

The mother does not agree finding that their son is too young for this and that
shared custody cannot occur before he is five years old.
[4]

[
8
]

In late October, the father petitions the
Superior Court to have his marriage annulled. The Court is not seized of this
matter.

[
9
]

On December 17, 2018, his access rights are
extended by a judgment on interim measures. He now has access to his son one
week-end every second week, from Friday afternoon to Monday morning when he
brings him to day care. The other week, he has access to him for the Friday
evening Shabbat supper; he picks up the child at day care and must return him
to his mother by 8:00 p.m. He is also authorized by the Court to go on a one
week vacation with his son to the Dominican Republic.

[
10
]

The parties agree that he will have a one week
holiday with his son during the summer and the mother also agrees that the son
and him travel to Disney World in Orlando for one week in September of 2019.

[
11
]

In August 2019, pursuant to a motion presented
by the father and a consent signed on the day of the hearing by the parties,
the child is registered in the Or A daycare, which is located in the same
complex as [A School].

[
12
]

In November 2019, the mother serves a motion for
divorce.

2.

ANALYSIS

2.1

Should the court grant shared custody?

[
13
]

The mother opposes shared custody as she feels
the child is too young and emotionally attached to her and because the father’s
parental philosophy does not adequately take into account the child’s emotional
needs.

[
14
]

She claims that the father’s increased access have
caused the child to become more aggressive physically and verbally. She also
indicates that the communication between the parents is very poor as the father
uses every opportunity to berate her and paper the file with lengthy emails
which she believes he intends to invoke in Court. She feels that the father is
taking positions in the written proceedings and in examinations and
representations before this Court which are uselessly bellicose, raising
irrelevant facts for the sole purpose of shaming her.

2.1.1

Legal principles

[
15
]

The Court must make its decision on shared
custody animated solely by the child’s best interest, taking into consideration
his moral, intellectual, emotional and physical needs, his age, his health, his
personality and his family environment.
[5]

[
16
]

Although not strictly seized with a motion for
provisional measures under the
Divorce Act
, it is worthy of note that

section 16(10)
of the
Divorce Act
specifies that the Court shall give
effect to the principle that a “child of the marriage should have as much
contact with each spouse as is consistent with the best interests of the child”.

[
17
]

Courts have consistently stated that there is no
presumption in favour of shared custody and that each application must be
evaluated taking into consideration the specific circumstances in which it is
presented.

[
18
]

To decide the issue of shared custody, the Court
will apply the factors recognized by the Court of Appeal in
Droit de la
famille — 16261
:

a) La capacité parentale et la
disponibilité des parents.

b) Le besoin
de stabilité de l’enfant.

c) La
proximité des résidences.

d) L’âge et
le désir de l’enfant lorsque applicable.

e) La
capacité minimale de communication des parents.

f)  L’absence
de mésentente systématique entre les parents.

g) L’existence
de valeurs éducatives, normales, spirituelles et de modes d’intervention
comparable en matière éducative.
[6]

[
19
]

For the reasons more fully set out hereunder,
the Court will grant shared custody on a seven day alternating basis.

2.1.2

The child’s age and desires

[
20
]

The child is too young to express his wishes.

[
21
]

In September 2018, the mother indicated that shared
custody could be envisaged in one and a half years. However, now, the mother’s
counsel argues that before the age of six, it is generally not advisable that
the child be in shared custody.

[
22
]

He refers to a doctrinal text of former Superior
Court Justice Louise Moreau and Mireille Pélissier-Simard, who cite
psychologists and a French psychiatrist as to the risk posed for a child
between 3 and 6 years old, given that the mother will be a “figure
d’attachement”.
[7]

The Court notes however that in a recent article published in the
Développements
récents en droit de la famille
, Frédéric Laterrière, a psychologist,
indicates that a 2-5-2-2-5 arrangement is best suited for children aged 3 to 5
while from six onwards, a 7-7 day arrangement is advisable.
[8]

[
23
]

The Court does not have the benefit of a
psychologist’s expertise and finds it hazardous to rely on extracts of
psychiatrists and psychologists opinions set out in doctrinal texts to determine
when shared custody is appropriate.

[
24
]

The Court finds it should rather be guided by
the comments made by the now associate chief justice, Catherine De La Rosa, in
Droit
de la famille – 08199
[9]
:

[34] La mère a déposé en plaidoirie
certains documents qui décrivent les dangers d’une garde partagée pour des
enfants en bas âge. Le Tribunal n’est pas d’accord avec une affirmation de
nature si générale. Chaque cas est un cas d’espèce. La garde partagée peut s’avérer
dans certaines circonstances tout à fait inadéquates, alors que dans d’autres
cas, elle est la solution la plus appropriée. Il n’y a pas de solution
parfaite. Chacune d’elle comporte des avantages et des inconvénients. Il faut
choisir les modalités de garde qui favorisent le meilleur intérêt de l’enfant
visé en relation avec sa propre réalité de vie et compter sur la collaboration
des parents pour amoindrir les inconvénients qui peuvent en découler.

[
25
]

No doubt, the notion of the “figure
d’attachement” of a very young child is a central concern for courts and may in
certain circumstances militate against shared custody.
[10]

[
26
]

The child is soon to be five years old. He attends
day care since a very young age and has changed day care three times. He has
spent significant time away from his mother over the last year. He stays with
his father from Friday to Monday morning every second week and they have gone,
together, on two one week trips to the Dominican Republic and to Orlando. He
spent one week in the summer with him.

[
27
]

Contrarily to the mother who lives with her
parents and relies heavily on them, the father, except for a single afternoon,
has been present systematically with the child throughout these periods.

[
28
]

If the mother was a “figure d’attachement” in August
2018 which perhaps could have warranted exclusive custody, since then, a
transition has occurred either consensually or imposed by the Court in December
2018. Given this transition, the child is now well prepared to adapt to shared
custody.

[
29
]

The mother has raised the fact that the child
cries in her absence and is sad. This behaviour manifests itself in the context
of
FaceTime
calls.

[
30
]

The parties have differing views on why this
occurs. The father says that the child relates that his mother is “fragile” and
that he must speak to her otherwise “she will be sad”. The mother indicates
that the child misses her and feels sad and that the father is not suited to
console him.

[
31
]

The interim measures on December 17, 2018
homologated the agreement entered into by the parties providing that the parent
who is not with the child may communicate with him via
Face Time
calls in
the morning between 7:15 a.m. and 8:15 a.m. and in the evening between 6:00 p.m.
and 7:30 p.m.

[
32
]

It does appear that because of their frequency
and their length, these calls have become counterproductive. In one instance, a
call on November 2, 2019 lasted over 80 minutes between the mother and the
child before the father insisted to put an end to the call.
[11]

[
33
]

In the aforementioned matter of
Droit de la
famille – 08199
,
justice De La Rosa

comments on how such calls can
be a double edged sword:
[12]

[44] Des contacts téléphoniques
peuvent être fixés de façon raisonnable; un à deux contacts paraissant une
fréquence adéquate. Il est important de mentionner que les contacts
téléphoniques ne doivent pas avoir l’effet d’empêcher l’enfant de s’adapter au
milieu de vie de l’autre parent, mais au contraire de favoriser le maintien et
le développement d’une relation significative de l’enfant avec le parent qui en
a la garde.

[45] Lorsque les contacts sont trop
nombreux, ils ont l’effet d’insécuriser l’enfant et de rompre la continuité de
ses activités. Bien entendu, il n’y a pas lieu d’empêcher de tels contacts
téléphoniques, mais il faut les exercer de façon raisonnable. Le parent qui
s’ennuie de ne pas avoir l’enfant avec lui doit penser au meilleur intérêt de
l’enfant et réaliser que l’ennui ressenti par le parent n’est pas
nécessairement éprouvé par l’enfant.

[
34
]

The frequency of the calls and the duration must
therefore be set more strictly and the Court will order that they can only
occur three times during a given week, for a maximum duration of 15 minutes
each.

2.1.3

Parental capacity and availability

2.1.3.1

Availability

[
35
]

The Court finds that both parents are equally
available for the child.

[
36
]

For the first two years, the mother insisted on
being with the child at all times and the father was relegated to take care of
all the meals, shop for groceries, clean the house and manage and pay the
bills.

[
37
]

This changes substantially when the child turns
three in 2018. The father must take an eight week medical leave and eventually resigns
from his employment in May 2018 to deal with an ongoing serious medical
condition.
[13]

This also coincides with the mother beginning to work again.

[
38
]

The father therefore takes on far greater
responsibilities. As mentioned above, he regularly picks his son up from the
day care in the early afternoon and spends time with him carrying out various
activities including going to the park and reading books to him. Also, when the
mother goes out with friends on Saturday evenings, he stays at home alone with
his son.

[
39
]

When they separate, the mother moves into her
parents’ house with her child where she resides since. Since the judgment on
interim measures, it is the maternal grandparents who pick the child up from
daycare towards 3:30 p.m. until the mother arrives at 5:30 p.m. It is the maternal
grandmother who is responsible for meals.

[
40
]

Having found an appropriate treatment for his
condition, the father accepts employment in August of 2018 as the […] of a
medical technology firm and he is responsible […]. He works mainly from home.
He starts his day very early to be aligned with Europe’s time zone and his work
is completed shortly before lunch. Both prior and after the interim judgment,
he takes full advantage of any access provided to him and only asked his
parents to step in once for a pick up at the day care, when he was rushed to
the hospital.

[
41
]

He has to travel on occasion for one week
business trips but has the freedom to schedule these trips when opportune
according to an eventual shared custody arrangement on alternating weeks.

2.1.3.2

Parent’s capabilities and educational norms and values

[
42
]

The Court is also convinced that both are
equally capable and loving parents who provide their child with significant quality
time, but in very different ways.

[
43
]

The Court does not see differences in parenting
philosophies as being inherently problematic. The parents will thereby provide
different perspectives which will enrich the child’s development.

[
44
]

The Court did not get a clear understanding of
the child’s routine or the activities he carries out after school and on
week-ends when he is with his mother, other than that he plays soccer and that
his grandparents play a great role. He seems to have a close relationship with
the mother’s sister and her two year old child who live in the Town A and who
visit the maternal grandparent’s house regularly. The child seems to live a
very sheltered life.

[
45
]

The Court has a much clearer sense of the father’s
views on parenting and the activities which he carries out with his son. In
summary, the father believes he must provide his son with an active and
intellectually challenging upbringing in a nurturing family setting all while
being mindful of his Jewish heritage and traditions.

[
46
]

A close relationship between the child and his
paternal grandparents is fostered and they spend every Friday together for a
Shabbat meal. Frequently, the father’s sister also attends this meal along with
her husband and daughter who is approximately the same age as the son.

[
47
]

He also judges that his son must be active just
as he has always been. In this regard, he encourages him to do sports. In early
2019 and in the Dominican Republic, the child follows tennis lessons with a
tennis pro. However, the child seems to prefer martial arts which the father exercises,
and he is given private lessons to master Muay Thai and Jiu Jitsu. In order
that the child does not injure himself or others, he carries out the sport one
on one with a professional and fights with pads. His father also takes him to a
slew of activities: amusement parks, auto and monster truck shows, fishing and
farm visits.

[
48
]

To foster his son’s cognitive development, and
given that the child is in a daycare up to August 2019 where all conversations
occur in Russian and he is living with the mother’s parents who always speak to
him in Russian, he concludes that the child insufficiently masters the English
and French language. He therefore registers him in the A Learning program to
improve his English.

[
49
]

He also impresses on the mother the importance
of a bilingual day care program and he is able to convince her eventually, on
the day of the hearing of a motion for issuance of a court order to such effect
in August 2019,
[14]

to register the child in the Or A CPE. This day care offers a bilingual
environment and is mindful of Jewish traditions. Jewish Holidays are celebrated
and certain prayers are recited in Hebrew.

[
50
]

He insists to be present to all dental and
medical appointments and is in fact present.

[
51
]

He therefore believes that this demonstrates
that his contribution is very different than that of the mother and that he
should have an equal role in his son’s life.

[
52
]

The mother objects to the child being involved
in martial arts, especially when it is not in a group with children of his age.
She believes it is inappropriate that he watch Ultimate Fighting Galas, as was
the case on November 2, 2019.

[
53
]

The grandmother relates that since the
separation, the child shows aggressive behaviour. The mother also testifies
that the child has, on two occasions, manifested violent behaviour, kicking a
fence on a farm visit and kicking his grandfather on one occasion behind the
leg for no reason, reproducing a move he would have learned in his martial arts
classes. The mother’s sister noticed that the child is becoming more aggressive
and is not as loving and caring as he was prior to the separation. She relates
as evidence one occasion where the child was rough with her daughter in relation
to a dispute regarding a toy.

[
54
]

The grandmother also relates that the child uses
four letter word expletives in English which she associates to the fact that he
frequents the father’s marital arts gym on a regular basis.

[
55
]

The father contends on the contrary that martial
arts allow his son to learn self-control and restraint. He points to a recent
event where a child bit the son’ arm in daycare. The daycare called the father
to report the incident and commented very favourably on the son’s very calm
response and restraint. When his father then commends him for his reaction, the
son explains that being strong and well-trained, it would be inappropriate for
him to fight back.

[
56
]

The father also says that the mother is applying
a double standard for the purposes of this hearing, as martial arts and combat
have always been part of the culture of the mother’s family and looked upon
favourably by the mother. In this regard he submits the following evidence:

56.1.

On November 11, 2014, while pregnant, the mother
writes to the father that she dreamed of their future son and she says that he
will have “bolls” and will box and do marshal [sic] arts”.
[15]

56.2.

On May 15, 2016, she posts a picture of the
maternal grandfather, the father and the one year old child in front of the TV,
with a heart and the caption: “Big boys …watching boxing”.
[16]

56.3.

On the father’s 40
th
birthday, she
buys him boxing gloves.

56.4.

The mother orders a semi-automatic assault
weapon for the maternal grandfather who is a former […] Army combatant and she proudly
poses with this weapon to which a bayonet is attached in the summer of 2016.
[17]

56.5.

The maternal grandfather is a hunter and has
many weapons in the house. He is the one who taught the father how to hunt and
fish, activities he has enthusiastically taken up.

56.6.

She posts a photo of her son on January 18, 2018
with the mention: “First martial arts class” with a thumbs up.
[18]

[
57
]

The Court must be wary of unduly interfering in a
parent’s educational choices.

[
58
]

The Court does not find it can draw any
conclusions on the negative impacts of martial arts on the child on the basis
on the few events which have been related in the Court matter.

[
59
]

The child is an active child of five years old
who is developing his personality in manners which may require some appropriate
disciplining. It is not unusual for a child that age to test the limits of his
parent’s patience.

[
60
]

The fact that a five year uses four letter words
is not wholly surprising and cannot automatically be linked to his presence at
the father’s gym.

[
61
]

The grandmother denies that swear words are ever
used in her home. The father contends that the maternal grandfather swears in
Russian and in French. In addition, the mother has been guilty of using very
foul language in her exchanges with the father.
[19]

[
62
]

Therefore, the Court concludes that the mother’s
criticisms are not warranted.

[
63
]

On the other hand, the Court, the Court also
finds that the father unduly criticizes the mother for being over concerned
with the child’s diet and imposing strict requirements, such as having the
child drink distilled water and not consume cold beverages or frozen ice cream.

[
64
]

The mother has been brought up in a different
cultural setting than the father which may explain differing views on such things
as air conditioning and beverage temperatures. Her views should not be
belittled.

[
65
]

The Court therefore believes that the parents’
values are sufficiently aligned to permit shared custody, but that they must
abstain to criticize the other party’s different views on education.

2.1.4

Stability

[
66
]

The Court does not believe that moving to shared
custody will destabilize the child.

[
67
]

As explained above, the father has been
omnipresent in the child’s life and all the more so since August 2018. The
father remains in the family home in which the child grew up. He has very close
contacts with his extended family who eat at the house often. He does not share
his life with a new partner.

[
68
]

The child mentions to his father that a
gentleman called Ma. F. is very much involved in the activities he carries out
with his mother. He comes along when they do outings. He is present when the
mother visits [B School], unbeknownst to the father, for the purpose of “taking
notes”. He assists the mother in drafting emails to the father.

[
69
]

Despite this substantial role, it was
surprisingly difficult throughout the testimony of the grandmother, the mother
and the sister to understand who this person is (including what his full name
is), what his employment, his address and his link to the family are. The grandmother
insists that this gentleman is simply a friend of the family, a neighbour who
is very often at the house. The sister contends that he is a very good friend
of her husband.

[
70
]

The Court reminds the parties that if this
gentleman takes on such an important role in the child’s life, this may have
impacts on the stability of the child’s surroundings and that transparency is
required.

2.1.5

Proximity of the parent’s domicile

[
71
]

The residences are 2.7 kilometers apart which
clearly allows for shared custody. In addition, the school that the Court will
order the child to attend is situated at the middle point of the two residences,
in walking distance of each. Hence, the child will have a coherent and stable
living environment.

2.1.6

Minimal capacity to communicate and systemic
disagreement

[
72
]

The parties’ relations are of course tainted by
the fact that the parties are wound up in a marriage annulment matter in which
the father makes very harsh statements.

[
73
]

The Court is not seized of that matter and
cannot comment on its merits. It does note that a motion to dismiss on the
grounds of
article 168
of the
Civil Code
of procedure was presented and
was dismissed.
[20]

[
74
]

Communication is not necessarily determinative
of the question of shared custody.
[21]

There must however be a minimum of communication between the parties.
[22]
The elements enumerated below
shows that there is such a minimum:

74.1.

They agree on medical and dental appointments
and generally will attend together; they exchange information on the child’s
health;
[23]

74.2.

They have agreed on the summer vacation and on
the fall trips to Orlando and Punta Cana;

74.3.

No evidence whatsoever has been filed on any
difficulties caused by the weekly drop-offs;

74.4.

They were able to find, albeit in a piecemeal
fashion, a resolution on the Jewish holidays;

74.5.

They communicated on day care and ultimately
agreed, even though on the day of a hearing, on the choice of Or A daycare;

74.6.

They have exchanged information on schools even
though they have not agreed.

[
75
]

The mother asserts that the communications with
the father are very poor, as she contends is demonstrated by emails she
produces and the evidence which the father has adduced which is meant to depict
her as being unreasonable and as having disturbing phobias.

[
76
]

The father responds that his emails are in
response to the mother’s email which are critical of his decisions and that he provides
in as much detail as is warranted. He also indicates that given that the mother
is contesting the shared custody namely on issues of communication and poor
parenting choices of the father, he must provide the Court with an exact picture
of the mother’s true beliefs and behaviour.

[
77
]

After careful review of the correspondence filed
by the mother, the Court does not share her reading thereof. The father has
access to the child since August 2018 and these emails show only few instances
of tense exchanges over a 15 month period. The father does react strongly on a
few occasions, but given the context, the tone remains civil and in most cases
a proper resolution of the fundamental matter at heart is found.

[
78
]

For example, it is clear that when the mother sends
an email entitled “X-unsupervised in pool”
[24]

and asserts that their son went under water and could not breathe, the father
will feel compelled to respond in detail if he feels this is inaccurate. Most
likely, the father is reading too much into the mother’s intentions in sending
her email, but the fact that this email was sent a mere ten days before the
hearing on the choice of daycare may in large part explain his great suspicion
of the mother’s motives.

[
79
]

The Court does not see anything improper with
the March 2019 exchange regarding the child’s appointment at the ear, nose and
throat specialist.

The mother explicitly
asks for the father’s input on medication proposed by the father which he does
provide, albeit in much more detailed fashion than the mother expected. The
exchange finishes on a constructive note.

[
80
]

It is also understandable that the father makes
his surprise known to the mother when he finds out that she attended a
trampoline amusement center, when she had asked him to stop going there a few
months prior because it was too dangerous for their son. The exchanges between
the parties, on this topic, were much too lengthy, diverted on other topics,
but both parties are to blame for this.

[
81
]

Finally, shortly before attending the hearing
herein, the parties write to one another on the choice of schools. Once again,
even though the parties have very detailed exchanges, the Court does not find
the father’s tone to be contemptuous or inappropriate.
[25]

[
82
]

The Court, therefore, cannot see these exchanges
as militating against shared custody. The parties will hopefully learn that such
written exchanges are not useful.

[
83
]

In order to ensure optimal communication, the
Court suggests that the parties keep a regular journal concerning the child to
be exchanged between them along with the child’s personal belongings. The
parents will note therein the child’s medical, school, and other appointments,
details concerning illness, medication, and particular problems requiring
weekly follow-ups.

[
84
]

It is also to further minimize any communication
difficulties that the Court does not accede to the mother’s subsidiary argument
for a 2-5-2-2-5 arrangement. This will increase the potential for disagreements
and will harm the child’s stability. An alternating week schedule which is
appropriate for the child’s age will offer less potential for friction.

2.1.7

Jewish Holidays

[
85
]

The parties have throughout the hearing provided
suggestions to the Court, which it has taken into consideration to come to its
conclusions.

2.2

Should the child be registered in the A School in the fall of 2020
or at the public elementary school?

[
86
]

The choice of school must be decided solely
based on the interest of the child.

[
87
]

[A School] is a private school but the father
agrees to pay for the school fees which total approximately $10,000 plus any
fundraising contributions. He contends that raising the child in the Jewish
tradition was agreed upon and [A School] will ensure this. He is of the opinion
that a child who graduates from [A School] has excellent prospects to enter
into the high school of his choice. [A School] is also linked to the daycare
which the child presently attends and this choice therefore guarantees
stability.

[
88
]

The mother wishes the child to attend either the
public neighbourhood school, [B School] which is part of the A School Board or
one of two private schools, which carry fees of $16,000 and $20,000
respectively and which she wants the father to pay for, and which she cannot pay.
She objects to [A School] on the grounds that given that her child is already
brought up in a trilingual environment, learning Hebrew would be
counterproductive. She also objects to what she refers to as the schools’
Jewish dogma, both on grounds of her religious belief, but also on the basis
that its strict adherence to Judaic practice and rituals will cause significant
organizational inconveniences, in particular regarding school closures on
holidays, early dismissal on Shabbat and Kashruth dietary laws.

[
89
]

The father has no fundamental objection
regarding [B School], but indicates that he has fears as to the stability of
the school in light of what he understands to be a dwindling English school
population. It also does not offer education on the Jewish tradition. He claims
that the parties had agreed to have their son attend a Jewish denominational
school.

[
90
]

The father has indicated that he is not willing
to pay for the very steep fees for the two private schools identified by the
mother. The Court therefore must decide between [A School] and [B School].

2.2.1

The academic programs of each school

[
91
]

[B School] is a public school part of the A
school board which offers various programs including a French Immersion program.
The child is admissible to attend this school as the father received his
elementary and high school education in Canada in English.

[
92
]

In kindergarten and grades 1 and 2, 85% of the instructional
time is in French, while in grades 3 to 6, the instructional time is shared
equally between French and English. Its students have very high pass rates in
their ministry exams in the final cycle.

[
93
]

School ends at 3:35 p.m. It offers subsidized daycare
from 7:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., which is also available on pedagogical days.

[
94
]

It is optimally situated at mid-point between
the parents’ domiciles.

[
95
]

[A School] offers a trilingual learning
environment. In kindergarten, the learning seems to be principally in French,
with 7.75 hours in Hebrew. In grades 1, 2 and 3, French remains dominant but
Hebrew occupies 9 hours of the weekly study program. [A School] prides itself
on the fact that 75% of its students make the honours society at west island
colleges and 98% of its graduates are accepted into their first choice of high
school.

[
96
]

[A School] dismissal time on Friday is at 2:45 p.m.
from November to March due to Shabbat and early sundown. There is an Extended
Day Program between the end of the school day and 6:00 p.m., but not on Fridays
from November to March and not on Holidays. In the 2019-2020 school year, aside
from civic holidays where schools province-wide are closed, [A School] is also
closed for Holidays in September for one day, in October for seven days over
four weeks, for five days in April and one day in May. The school also has
professional afternoons on eight afternoons and two days for Staff Professional
days.

[
97
]

[A School] is a denominational school. Its
program encompasses three pillars of “Jewish Living” which it approaches
through “meaningful experiences and explorations rooted in classical studies,
Tradition and the centrality of Medinat Yisreal”.
[26]

[
98
]

At lunchtime, the students must follow the
“customs of hand washing and saying the Brachot and Birkat Hamazon”. They must
abide by the dietary laws of Kashruth and all food must bear a recognized
Kashruth symbol. On Monday, Wednesday and Friday, the school allows
dairy/pareve lunches and snacks, while on Tuesday and Thursday, it allows
Pareve/meat lunches and snacks. For boys, the wearing of the kippah is part of
the mandatory dress code.
[27]

[
99
]

Presently, the child attends pre-kindergarden at

Garderie d’Or A
as a result of an agreement between the parties signed
on August 1, 2019. This school is part of the same building complex than [A
School] and the Beth Tikvah Congregation. It is a bilingual day care. Jewish
holidays are celebrated and the children are initiated to Jewish holidays and
rites and customs.

2.2.2

The child’s best interest

[
100
]

The choice of school must be decided taking into consideration
school transportation, the parent’s presence, the child’s stability, the
school’s proximity and the costs related to each school.
[28]

[
101
]

An additional level of complexity is added in this matter as the
father wishes the child to be educated in a Jewish denominational school while
the mother opposes this.

[
102
]

The child cannot yet opine on what his desires are regarding his
religious education.  The matter is therefore pleaded through the prism of the
parent’s religious beliefs.

[
103
]

In
Big M. Drug Mart
, the Supreme Court states that “the
essence of the concept of freedom of religion is the right to entertain such
religious beliefs as a person chooses (…) and the right to manifest religious
belief by worship and practice”.
[29]

As a corollary, the Supreme Court also indicates that “no one is to be forced
to act in a way contrary to his beliefs or his conscience”.
[30]

[
104
]

Denominational schools are an integral part of Quebec’s distinct
educational landscape, where two parallel streams of denominational and secular
public schools cohabitate. As explained by the Supreme Court in
Loyola
,
[31]
the core curriculum of private
denominational schools, just as that of public schools are regulated by the
province and is compulsory according to the
Education Act
.

[
105
]

The choice to place a child in a denominational school poses no problem
if the parents agree.

[
106
]

However, here they appear not agree. In family matters, the
religious freedoms of the parents must be exercised in the child’s best
interest.

[
107
]

The father contends that there is an agreement or an expectation
that child would be attending a denominational Jewish school. He argues that
right from their very first exchanges via text message, the Jewish faith and
traditions play an important role. There was never any doubt during the parties’
common life that the child would be brought up in the Jewish faith and that
this would include attending a Jewish denominational school.

[
108
]

The mother who professes to adhere to the Jewish Faith, says she is
does not practice its rites and customs. Her parents never did. Only the
Christian Orthodox New Year was celebrated when she grew up. She argues never
to have committed to having her son raised in strict observance of Jewish rites
and traditions in a denominational school. She agrees to celebrate a Jewish
wedding to accommodate the father and he is the one of drives the whole process
by which her Jewish lineage was to be established for this purpose. During
their common life, other than a few “quick” Shabbat suppers and a few
attendances at synagogues, they do not abide to rituals, nor do they eat Kosher
or pareve meals. She even seems to call into question the fact that the father
carries out his daily prayers with prayer boxes (tefillin). She therefore seems
to contend that the father’s insistence on having the child raised according to
Judaic tradition and customs is part of a newfound religious sentiment which is
not present when they date, marry or live together.

[
109
]

The Court finds that the mother’s reticence to have the child attend
a denominational school is somewhat incoherent with her behaviour before,
during and after the union including during the proceedings. On the other hand,
the father has consistently shown his attachment to the Jewish faith and the
central role it plays in his life.

[
110
]

In their first exchange, the father indicates that he wears the
tefillin (philactaries) every morning for prayers and that he tries to go to
his parents or to the rabbis on Fridays.
[32]

The mother replies that she used to go to the synagogue a few years ago, but
not anymore.
[33]

[
111
]

When she announces she is pregnant in August 2019, it is a priority
of the couple that they be wed in the Jewish faith in a traditional Jewish
wedding. The father explains, and this is not contested by the mother, that in
order to be admitted in the Jewish faith, a child must be born from a Jewish
union celebrated in the Judaic tradition; otherwise, he will be considered a
“Mamzer”.

[
112
]

However, the mother’s father is Russian Christian Orthodox while her
mother is the daughter of a Jewish mother. Her parents did not marry according
to Judaic tradition. Therefore, the rabbis who will celebrate the parties’
wedding require that the mother either convert formally or prove her Jewish
lineage. The mother objects to converting contending she is Jewish and
therefore opts to prove her Jewish lineage and, with the father’s help,
proceeds to prepare an extensive dossier required in this regard.

[
113
]

The grandmother attends three meetings to provide details regarding
her mother, the child’s great grandmother, including the fact that she was an
Auschwitz survivor. The mother goes so far as asking a third party, apparently
unbeknownst to the father, to alter the photo of the great grandmother’s
tombstone to add a Judaic star.
[34]

[
114
]

Written submissions are provided to the Russian Jewish Community
where the mother relates that she attended synagogues in her youth. She
indicates that she and the father want their children to grow up with Jewish
values, that their son is to have a brit [the Jewish
Brit milah

circumcision ritual] and that he be “raised according to all the Jewish
customs”.
[35]

[
115
]

Before the child is born, the mother, while relating that she dreamt
of their soon to be born child, asks the father about information regarding the
[C School] on [...], which is a denominational school.

[
116
]

When X is born, he is given the biblical names X. He is circumcised
in accordance with Jewish Law and Tradition.
[36]

[
117
]

Two days after the child is born, the father pre-registers him with
the Centre de la Petite Enfance (CPE) Or [Center A] on the provincial central
registration system, […].
[37]

[
118
]

In August 2016, the parents attend [A School]’s BBQ. The father
sends a thank you note the purpose is evidently to endear his family to [A
School] to ensure registration in due course. The mother replies: “very nice”.
[38]

[
119
]

After they separate and during the Court proceedings, she insists
that the child celebrate Jewish holidays with her. During her examination on
November 20, 2019, lengthy exchanges ensure to determine which of the Seder
suppers she will be able to spend with her son for each of the Jewish high holidays.
She also wants to ensure that she can attend the Purim celebrations with the
child at the synagogue and that she can light the candles of the menorah on
several nights of Hanukkah.

[
120
]

Also, in her Introductory Demand for Divorce and Accessory Measures she
asks that the father be ordered to grant her the
get
. The Supreme Court’s
description of the
get
’s function in
Bruker
v.
Markowitz
[39]
demonstrates that it is a
matter of concern for a woman who observes Jewish Law.

[
121
]

The Court finds that the parties clearly intended to bring the child
in a setting where the Judaism and Judaic rites and traditions play an
important role and that it would be logical that the child attend a
denominational school.

[
122
]

However, the Court cannot dismiss the linguistic and organizational
reserves she raises with regard to [A School].

[
123
]

Although it is a great asset to be a polyglot, the child whose other
tongue appears to be Russian, is having certain challenges to master English
and this has led to him following English tutorials at A learning. He will have
to learn French, which he presently does not truly speak. To add Hebrew during
eight hours per week also does not appear realistic. In addition, the parents
do not speak Hebrew and assisting their child with his homework in a shared
custody setting will be complex.

[
124
]

Furthermore, there are frequent school closures during Jewish Holidays.
In addition, from November to March, school closes on Fridays at 2:30 p.m. for
Shabbat. Also, there is no guarantee that during Staff Professional Days and
early dismissals, daycare is provided. The father has offered that he could
take care of the child at all such times. Given the non-optimal communications
between the parties, the Court finds that such an arrangement is unrealistic
and not advisable.

[
125
]

Also, the Kastruth dietary requirements pose important challenges
for the mother. She indicates that it will be difficult for her to follow the
strict rules that it implies. Her option is to sign up for the meal plan.
However, as was put in evidence, the mother is very concerned that her son eat
healthy, including organically sourced food. If he is in a meal plan, she is
prevented from ensuring that he eats what she believes is best for him.

[
126
]

For these reasons, the Court finds that [B School] elementary school
is the most appropriate choice. It must also be noted that [B School] is in
walking distance of both homes which will strengthen the child’s sense of attachment
to his community.

2.2.3

After school program

[
127
]

The Court is however mindful of the importance for the child to be
well integrated in the Jewish faith and community. The Court therefore asked
the parties to look into after school programs where the child will be
familiarized with the Hebrew faith and tradition. The program B at the CPE of the
Y in Town A was found to be suitable by them.

[
128
]

They both undertake to have the child participate in this program
and they will drop the child and pick him up from the CPE of the Y during the
week in which they have custody of the child.

[
129
]

On the last day of the hearings, the father identified another
public school, [D School], in the A School Board, also close to the parents’
domiciles, which offers an after school program in Hebraic traditions.

[
130
]

Unfortunately, the parents do not reside in this school’s district.
It is possible for the school board to accept a transfer to this school, on
application, but the Court cannot order the child to attend such school. It
will be for the parties to decide whether this is an option they wish to
explore by consent.

2.3

Adjustments to the alimony

[
131
]

The parties have agreed that their respective revenues for the
purpose of calculating the alimony payable are $171,648 for the father and
$55,000 for the mother.

[
132
]

The father will therefore pay an alimony of $347 per month to the mother
for the benefit of the child.
